title: What does COP31 reveal about the geopolitics of climate change?
gist: Chatham House argues COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, though record-attended (93,000 participants), reveals a geopolitical shift: the US has fully exited the climate regime, Europe, the UK and Canada are retreating domestically and stalling climate finance, while China (29.5% of 2025 emissions) wins Global South favour by exporting clean tech. Real transition drivers, including the Iran war's boost to low-carbon tech, matter more than conference outcomes.

themes.theme: COP31 turnout vs. eroding climate politics

insights.claim: COP31 in Turkey drew a record 93,000 registered participants and 77 heads of state and government, even as the developed-world political right rejects climate action and corporations drop net zero targets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Summit headcount signals climate's global salience persists despite Western political retreat; don't read Western ESG pullback as global demand collapse.
insights.quote: A record 93,000 participants as well as 77 heads of state and governments registered to attend.

insights.claim: Corporations are dropping net zero targets and fossil fuel companies are scrapping or scaling back their low-carbon divisions, while even centre and centre-left leaders deprioritize emissions cuts.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Oil majors' low-carbon retreat reduces corporate clean-energy capex in the West; transition growth must come from elsewhere (China, Global South).
insights.quote: And fossil fuel companies are scrapping or scaling back their low-carbon divisions.
insights.locator: Today, much of the political right

insights.claim: COP negotiating frameworks are frozen in early-1990s categories: Gulf states are still classed as 'developing' despite top per-capita wealth, and developing countries demand technology transfer even though China, itself 'developing', dominates clean technology.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Climate-finance and tech-transfer negotiations are structurally misaligned with economic reality, limiting expectations for meaningful COP finance outcomes.

insights.claim: The flagship COP31 electrification target proposed by hosts Australia and Turkey will not require the electricity to come from low-carbon sources, a consequence of continued fossil fuel lobbying influence, despite the clear cost advantage of low-carbon power.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Electrification target is fuel-agnostic, so it is neutral-to-positive for gas generation demand as well as renewables; watch the final text.
insights.quote: Such a stipulation is basically off the table in Antalya, a consequence of the continued influence of fossil fuel interests.

themes.theme: US exit and Trump energy dominance

insights.claim: The US has no delegation at COP31: President Trump formally withdrew from the Paris Agreement in 2025 and from the underlying UN climate convention in 2026, following Biden's reengagement and Trump's first-term Paris exit in 2017.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Full US exit from the UNFCCC removes the largest historical emitter from multilateral climate finance; US climate policy whipsaws with each administration.
insights.locator: The most extreme example is the United States.

insights.claim: US climate policy whipsaws because it is shaped by two forces: the superpower contest with China (which briefly drove a low-carbon 'race-to-the-top' via the Inflation Reduction Act) and the US's new position as the world's leading oil and gas producer, which Trump's 'energy dominance' strategy exploits.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: US policy favors hydrocarbons over renewables under Trump; clean-tech policy support is cyclical and tied to US-China rivalry framing.
insights.quote: But policy is also influenced by the US’s newfound position as the world’s leading oil and gas producer.
insights.locator: This whipsaw climate policy is influenced

themes.theme: Europe and middle powers in retreat

insights.claim: The EU has dialled down COP31 expectations largely due to US absence; EU climate diplomat Wopke Hoestra called for a narrow focus on the electrification target and dismissed further finance talks as 'dead in the water'.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Climate finance expansion is effectively stalled among major donors; lower odds of new multilateral finance flows to emerging markets.
insights.quote: dismissing any further talks on finance as ‘ dead in the water ’
insights.locator: The EU, traditionally among the most ambitious

insights.claim: European leaders are distracted by the Russian threat: most skipped the Antalya World Leaders' Summit to attend a security-focused European Political Community meeting in Dublin.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Security spending is crowding out climate in European political bandwidth; defence over decarbonization as the policy priority.
insights.locator: Europe’s political class is also distracted

insights.claim: Canada and the UK pair international climate-finance pledges with domestic retreat: Canada under Mark Carney has dismantled climate policies and funded new fossil fuel infrastructure, while the UK under Andy Burnham approved new gas drilling and is considering weakening EV targets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Domestic policy tilts toward fossil supply (Canadian infrastructure, UK gas drilling) and softer EV mandates; negative for UK EV adoption pace.
insights.quote: But this international positioning is paired with domestic retreat.
insights.locator: Canada and the UK, positioning themselves

insights.claim: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told COP31 the climate consensus had 'gone', but this is a UK-centric view: cross-party support collapsed in Westminster while a record 75% of the global population considers climate change a serious threat.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Western political consensus loss is not mirrored globally; global demand for climate action remains high outside rich-country politics.
insights.quote: But a record share of the global population ( 75 per cent ) considers climate change a serious threat.
insights.locator: Burnham did attend the COP leaders’ summit.

themes.theme: Global South: transition as growth play

insights.claim: Developing countries in South-East Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and Latin America are treating the low-carbon economy as a growth opportunity and rolling out renewables at a rate that will soon match or exceed rich-world peers.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Renewable demand growth is shifting to emerging markets; favors suppliers (largely Chinese) and EM project developers over Western-policy-dependent plays.
insights.locator: First, many are treating the new low-carbon economy

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia, which has long blocked COP progress and did so again in Antalya, used COP31 to announce a major wind and solar deal with host Turkey.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Even petrostates hedge into renewables commercially while obstructing diplomatically; watch Gulf capital flowing into regional wind/solar.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia, which has long blocked progress

insights.claim: Very few developed countries renewed climate-finance pledges after they expired in 2025, despite pledging to lead scaling climate finance to $300 billion by 2035, while adaptation and loss-and-damage finance becomes central to talks.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Gap between $300bn 2035 goal and renewed pledges deepens North-South distrust and leaves room for China to fill financing gaps.
insights.quote: However, very few developed countries have renewed their financial pledges after they expired in 2025.

themes.theme: China as clean-tech supplier and emitter

insights.claim: China accounted for 29.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025, the largest share by some distance, while deploying low-carbon technologies at breathtaking speed and scale.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: China is simultaneously the decisive emitter and decisive clean-tech deployer; its trajectory dominates global emissions outcomes.

insights.claim: China's 2026 clean tech exports (solar panels, batteries, EVs) will cut emissions equivalent to Brazil's annual emissions, and Beijing frames these exports as its core contribution to global climate efforts.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Chinese clean-tech export volumes are large and politically framed as climate leadership, supporting continued export expansion into the Global South.
insights.quote: the country’s clean tech exports in 2026 will cut emissions equivalent to what Brazil emits in a year
insights.locator: It is exporting its solar panels

insights.claim: As developed countries fail on climate finance and slow domestic efforts, China, styling itself leader of the developing world, supplies the means to transition and invests heavily in clean tech manufacturing abroad, winning an ever-warmer reception in the Global South.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Structural shift of clean-tech influence and market share to China; Chinese overseas manufacturing investment is a key trend for EM supply chains.
insights.quote: China is receiving an ever-warmer reception, through its clean technology, its investments, and its relative stability as an international climate actor.
insights.locator: Here is where climate and geopolitics

insights.claim: China is reportedly part of an effort with Saudi Arabia, Russia, India and Kenya to delay work on crucial climate science at the talks.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: China's climate posture is commercial, not purely altruistic; diplomatic obstruction coexists with clean-tech export push.

themes.theme: Iran war and real-economy transition drivers

insights.claim: The Iran war has made low-carbon technology more attractive in many parts of the world, as energy security concerns reinforce the transition independent of COP outcomes.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Oil-supply shocks from Middle East conflict act as a demand catalyst for renewables and EVs in import-dependent countries.
insights.quote: The Iran war has made low-carbon technology more attractive in many parts of the world.
insights.locator: Separating the signal from the noise

insights.claim: COP outcomes give a distorted and dissatisfying picture of climate efforts; investors and analysts should look past conference results to real-world energy transition progress and geopolitical shifts.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Don't trade COP headlines; track deployment data, trade flows and geopolitics for the transition signal.
insights.quote: But focusing on conference outcomes alone ignores real world progress on the energy transition
insights.locator: But focusing on conference outcomes alone
